title: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM MOSES’ STAFF
paragraphs: THE LESSON I LEARNED FROM MOSES’ STAFF
Some of the most powerful things God uses look completely ordinary.
Just a shepherd's staff weathered by years of desert dust, sweat, loneliness, and obscurity.

Yet that ordinary staff would one day split seas, confront empires, bring water from rocks, display the judgment of God, reveal His mercy, and become one of the most recognizable symbols of divine authority in all Scripture.
What if the greatest lesson of Moses’ staff is not about the staff at all?
What if it is about what happens when God takes something ordinary, surrendered, and seemingly insignificant and transforms it into an instrument of His glory?
Because that is exactly what Jesus still does today.
And perhaps that is exactly what He wants to do with you.
The story begins in a place few people would envy.
He had once lived in the courts of Egypt, surrounded by privilege and opportunity. But after killing an Egyptian and fleeing for his life, he spent decades in Midian as a shepherd.
Forty years of wondering whether his best days had already passed.
Exodus 4 records one of the most profound moments in biblical history.
God asked Moses a simple question.
In Hebrew, the word used is מַטֶּה (matteh).
The term can mean a staff, rod, branch, tribal authority, or symbol of leadership.
The object represented far more than a walking stick.
Everything he believed he possessed was wrapped up in that simple answer.
The moment Moses obeyed, the staff became a serpent.
When he obeyed again and picked it up, it became a staff once more.
God was teaching Moses a lesson that echoes through every generation.
What remains in our hands is ordinary.
What is surrendered into God's hands becomes extraordinary.
The miracle was never in the wood.
The miracle was in the God who commanded it.
Many believers spend years praying for greater purpose while tightly gripping the very things God has asked them to surrender.
We want God to bless what remains under our control.
But throughout Scripture, God works through surrender.
The staff had to leave Moses' hand before it could become an instrument of divine power.
The same principle appears throughout the Gospel.
This is the rhythm of God's kingdom.
Lose your life and find it.
Die to self and live in Christ.
Surrender control and discover true freedom.
Jesus expressed this beautifully in John 12:24:
“Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.”
The Kingdom of God often begins where human control ends.
Years later, the staff appeared again.
When Moses stood before Pharaoh, it was in his hand.
When plagues struck Egypt, it was in his hand.
When Israel stood trapped between Pharaoh's army and the Red Sea, it was in his hand.
“Lift up your staff, and stretch out your hand over the sea and divide it.”
The sea did not part because of Moses.
The sea did not part because of the staff.
The sea parted because God was present.
Yet God chose to work through something Moses had already surrendered.
There is a profound truth hidden here.
God rarely asks us to become someone else.
He asks us to surrender what we already have.
Too often believers compare themselves to others.
Meanwhile God asks the same question He asked Moses.
Not what is in someone else's hand.
Not what you wish you possessed.
Not what you might receive someday.
What is already in your hand?
The kingdom advances when surrendered people place ordinary things into extraordinary hands.
The Hebrew Scriptures repeatedly reveal this pattern.
A jar of oil in a widow's hand.
Five loaves and two fish in a boy's hand.
The issue was never the object.
God is not searching for impressive tools.
He is searching for surrendered hearts.
Perhaps the most beautiful lesson from Moses' staff emerges later in Israel's journey.
God instructed Moses to speak to the rock.
Instead, Moses struck it with the staff.
The staff itself possessed no magical power.
Its purpose was never to replace God's voice.
It was merely a symbol pointing beyond itself.
This remains a danger for every generation.
We can begin trusting methods more than God.
The staff was valuable only because it pointed to the One who held ultimate authority.
The same is true for ministries, churches, leaders, books, platforms, and accomplishments.
None of them are the source.
The New Testament reveals the ultimate fulfillment of everything Moses' staff represented.
All of it finds its completion in Jesus Christ.
The Greek word used repeatedly for authority in the New Testament is ἐξουσία (exousia).
It describes delegated power, rightful authority, and sovereign rule.
“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to Me.”
Moses delivered Israel from earthly slavery.
Jesus delivers humanity from the slavery of sin.
Moses pointed people toward the Promised Land.
Jesus is the way into the eternal Kingdom of God.
Every symbol ultimately points to Him.
Every story ultimately leads to Him.
This is why the lesson of Moses' staff is so personal.
The enemy constantly whispers that your past disqualifies you.
That is our theme because it is God's pattern.
Maybe you have spent years believing your life is too broken, too messy, too ordinary, or too late to matter.
His staff reminds us that God often begins His greatest work in places the world overlooks.
The question is not whether you possess something extraordinary.
The question is whether you are willing to surrender what is already in your hand.
Because when surrendered people place ordinary things into the hands of an extraordinary Savior, history changes.
Perhaps today Jesus is asking you the same question He asked Moses.
But God's plans rarely begin with human impressiveness.
If this message stirred something deep within you, do not keep it to yourself.
What is the "staff" God has placed in your hand?
What have you been afraid to surrender?
Your testimony may become the encouragement someone else desperately needs today.
One surrendered life in the hands of Jesus can accomplish more than a thousand gifted lives clinging to control.
